overview: Takrur was an influential kingdom and commercial center in the Senegal River valley, especially prominent in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Its name later traveled far beyond its original homeland. The map’s 1000 to 1279 span selects part of that medieval history; it should not be confused with the separate eighteenth-century label “Tekrur”.

periods.title: A Muslim court in the Senegal valley
periods.summary: War Jabi adopted Islam and promoted Islamic law during the eleventh century.

periods.title: Trade and regional power
periods.summary: Takrur linked the Senegal valley with Saharan commerce before Mali’s ascendancy.

periods.title: A name with a wider life
periods.summary: The name increasingly designated West African Muslims abroad, beyond the original kingdom.

items.text: War Jabi’s adoption of Islam in the eleventh century mattered politically as well as religiously. Arabic writers connect his reign with Islamic law. A ruler’s conversion tells us about court policy; the region’s religious life developed over a longer and more varied history.

Al-Idrisi’s twelfth-century account describes merchants arriving with wool, copper and other goods, and leaving with gold and enslaved people. Trade brought wealth and far-reaching contacts, but also depended on coercion and the forced movement of people.

A later Arabic description by al-Qazwini presents Takrur as a large, unwalled town containing Muslims and followers of other religions. This is a reminder that medieval authors did not always give the same picture: towns and communities changed, and reports had different sources.

Sincu Bara is a major archaeological site in the wider Senegal valley, covering roughly 67 hectares. It helps reveal the society from which medieval states emerged. Its precise relationship to named capitals remains uncertain, so its finds are regional evidence rather than a labeled royal household.

Copper-alloy finds from Sincu Bara include rings, decorated disks and bells. Scientific analysis distinguishes brass, leaded brass and copper. A glittering ornament was the result of skilled material choices, not simply a lump of metal beaten into whatever shape happened to appear.

New excavations in 1991 and 1992 changed the site’s story. Researchers placed the arrival of copper-based metals around 800 to 900 CE, later than earlier estimates. Separating disturbed layers helped reveal change that had previously been mistaken for centuries of sameness.

Iron smelting was another substantial regional skill. David Killick studied furnace residues and radiocarbon dates from several Senegal valley sites, spanning many centuries. These remains preserve the work of people controlling fire, ore and airflow, essential skills behind useful metal objects.

Charred seeds from seven Senegal valley sites show pearl millet as the most common identified crop in nearly every examined assemblage. The strongest occupation evidence largely predates 1000 CE. These small remains reveal the agricultural foundations supporting the later medieval communities.

People also used wild plants. Jujube fruit was abundant in some excavated communities and scarce in others, alongside varied grasses and tree fruits. Even within one river valley, dinner did not follow a single standard menu: local resources and choices mattered.

sections.title: Writing and a name that traveled

items.text: Here is the name in Arabic: “تكرور”, or “Takrur”. This spelling is printed as the headword of the 2011 scholarly encyclopedia entry. Arabic authors discussed the kingdom in medieval geographical works; this is a modern printed witness to the name, not a newly discovered medieval inscription.

Historian Umar al-Naqar traced how the name broadened among pilgrims and migrants in the Middle East. It could refer to West African Muslims who came from far outside the original kingdom. The reputation of a place sometimes travels farther than the armies of its rulers.

This wider meaning caused confusion even in medieval times. Al-Naqar discusses an account in which Mali’s Mansa Musa objected to being called ruler of Takrur, since Takrur was only part of his much larger realm. Names on maps need context as well as spelling.

ending.text: Takrur lost its earlier predominance as Mali expanded during the thirteenth century. The imported 1279 endpoint is not a securely established single destruction date. Its communities continued, and the name retained a much broader life in Muslim geography and identity.
